newsitem.title: USA: Bank of Ireland suit accuses bar of taking its name.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Ireland suit accuses bar of taking its name.

text.p: A San Francisco bar and restaurant has upset a 200-year-old Irish bank by calling itself "The Bank of Ireland."
The dispute peaked recently when the Dublin-based Bank of Ireland sued the owners of the one-year-old bar, the bar's co-owner Chris Martin said on Wednesday.
The suit accuses the pub of misappropriating its name and asks the U.S. District Court here to stop it using the name.
The bank said in papers filed in court that it had used the name "Bank of Ireland" since 1783 and the bar's use of it "taints the bank's reputation."
"The bank does not wish to be affiliated in any way with the sale of alcohol under its name, or with the sale of food (such as the "Bank of Ireland Burger")," the lawsuit says.

Martin opened the bar and restaurant with fellow Dubliner Rory Connolly last January. They chose the name because it was in the heart of San Francisco's financial district and because they wanted to distinguish it from the city's many other Irish bars. They later created an Internet site, advertising the restaurant.

But in August, a legal adviser for the Bank of Ireland sent the tavern a letter asking it to immediately stop using the name. After various exchanges and offers of compromise between the two sides, the bank sued in late November, seeking to stop the bar from using the name as well as unspecified "monetary remedies."
Terence Redmond, attorney for the restaurant, said the financial institution, which has a U.S. branch in New York, wanted to avoid confusion among the public about the name.
"If they had a retail location here or if they at least advertised in California ... that would kind of make sense, but they have no presence," Redmond said.
But the bank said in the suit that it had significant business contacts with California, including more than $100 million in loans to California lenders.
Martin said the bar's owners believed they had a valid case but would probably have to give up the name because of the prohibitive costs of fighting the case in court.
The bar had already taken its name off the Internet and negotiations continued, Martin added.
